speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: PRESENCE IN SPEAKERS GALLERY OF FRENCH DELEGATES TO MEETING OF FRANCE-CANADA INTERPARLIAMENTARY ASSOCIATION
speechtext:
This year, the France-Canada Interparliamentary Association is holding its meetings in Ottawa. During the next few days, French and Canadian parliamentarians, members of the French National Assembly and the Canadian House of Commons, will be discussing topics of mutual interest.
It gives me great pleasure to point out to the House the presence in the Speaker's gallery of the members of the French delegation. This delegation, led by the Questor, Mr. Lucien Neuwirth, represents the complete range of political groupings in the National Assembly. On behalf of hon. members, I extend a warm welcome to our distinguished visitors. On behalf of my colleagues, I also wish them a pleasant stay in Canada, particularly in Ottawa, Montreal, Perce and Gaspe, where they will spend a few hours on the weekend. Those who take an interest in the work of this association are confident that the talks at this meeting will help strengthen the ties of friendship which already link France and Canada so closely.

STORAGE OF NATURAL GAS AND PETROLEUM-REQUEST FOR UNANIMOUS CONSENT TO MOVE MOTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the uncertainty which prevails in Canada over the oil situation, we feel that we must urgently request the adjournment of the House, and considering that building a pipeline between the Arctic Islands and Montreal would be more advantageous than building a liquefaction plant in the Arctic and transporting gas in tankers all the way to the Magdelen Islands, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Allard), under Standing Order 43:
That this House do now adjourn to carry out the necessary inquiry into the storing of natural gas and oil within the scope of a storing policy similar to that enforced by the United States so as to better serve eastern Canada and accumulate stocks to prevent any shortage which might result from an international crisis with the producing countries.

subsubtopic: AIR CANADA-TRAVEL INSURANCE
speechtext:
1.	For what insurance company or companies does Air Canada act as agent?
2.	What kinds of insurance are available?

4.	Does the government agree that any insurance company that Air Canada does, or will in future, act as an agent should be Canadian?

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: AIR CANADA-TRAVEL INSURANCE
speechtext:
The management of Air Canada advises as follows: 1. Air Canada acts as agent for Voyageur Travel Insurance Ltd. With respect to insurance on air cargo, the corporation
acts for the Insurance Company of North America.
2.	World-Wide Travel Accident, All-Risk Baggage, Air Flight, and Trip Cancellation. With respect to air cargo, there is available shippers' all risk against physical damage and carrier's legal liability to a declared value by the shipper.
3.	The procedure follows that used by the air transportation industry generally. Air Canada negotiates with an insurance broker to become a handling agent. When terms are agreed a letter of agreement is concluded.
4.	The Ministry of Transport advises as follows: Air Canada, as a Crown corporation, has the responsibility to negotiate with the insurance companies, and would no doubt take into consideration the nationality of the companies concerned as well as the rate structure.

subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: EMPLOYEES OF 1971-72 LIP PROGRAM
speechtext:
1.	How many employees of the 1971-72 LIP Program were already employed when they started work on a LIP project?
2.	How many were receiving unemployment insurance?
3.	How many were on welfare?
4.	How many were registered at Manpower Centres?
5.	How many were farmers?

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: EMPLOYEES OF 1971-72 LIP PROGRAM
speechtext:
Definitive data such as requested was not maintained by the Program in 1971-72. Some information is available from an analysis, collected on the basis of employee questionnaires. Of an estimated 92,000 workers in the 1971-72 program: 1. Approximately 15,000 were employed prior to starting work on LIP projects. Of this 15,000, 38 per cent were employed part-time; 30 per cent were on lay-off; 26 per cent were in a slack period with little or no income, e.g., farmers, fishermen; 3 per cent not classified; 3 per cent who may have left full-time jobs to take LIP work.
2.	Approximately 23,000 employees reported their main source of income, prior to LIP, to be from Unemployment Insurance benefits.
3.	Approximately 11,000 employees reported their main source of income, prior to LIP, to be from welfare.
4.	LIP workers were not required to be registered at Manpower Centres in the 1971-72 Program.
5.	Farmers were not recorded as such but approximately 24,000 workers were recorded in the category "Farming, Fishing, Forestry or Mining".

speechtext:

4.	Does the government actually contribute their share to the fund, or is it merely a book entry?

6.	What was the total amount paid out of the Public Service Superannuation Account for the fiscal years ending (a) March 31, 1971 (b) March 31, 1972 (c) March 31, 1973 as pension benefits?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. M. Drury (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE SUPERANNUATION ACCOUNT
speechtext:
All of the information requested in respect of the fiscal year which ended on March 31, 1973 is not yet available. 1. The total amount in the Public Service Superannuation Account was: (a) $3,990.0 million at March 31, 1971; (b) $4,488.5 million at March 31, 1972.
2.	Interest is credited to the Public Service Superannuation Account on a quarterly basis in each fiscal year in respect of the balance to the credit of the Superannuation Account on the last day of each quarter. Such interest is calculated as if all contributions made to the Superannuation Account in each quarter less the amount paid from the account in that quarter had been invested since the account started in 1924, on a basis similar to that applied under the Canada Pension Plan, and as if those amounts were re-invested at current rates every 20 years. The rate of interest used for the account as a whole is the weighted average rate for the amounts so invested in respect of each quarter. Accordingly, the rate can change every quarter. At present the Canada Pension Plan rate is equal to the average yield on government of Canada bonds with 20 or more years to maturity so that new funds and reinvested funds from 1953 are currently earning interest at the rate of 7.26 per cent. Interest earned by the excess of the quarterly interest rate over one per cent is applied as required by law to form part of the amortization payments

required to reduce actuarial deficiencies arising primarily out of salary increases. Such additional interest in the amount of $49.5 million and $65.3 million was applied in this way during the fiscal years 1970-1971 and 1971-1972, respectively.
3.	(a) The amount of interest credited to the Public Service Superannuation Account was: (i) $147.7 million during the fiscal year 1970-1971 plus the $49.5 million additional interest applied as described in (2) above; (ii) $163.7 million during the fiscal year 1971-1972 plus the $65.3 million additional interest applied as described in (2) above; (b) The average rate of interest was 5.3460 per cent for the fiscal year 1970-1971, 5.5895 per cent for the fiscal year 1971-1972 and 5.8969 per cent for the fiscal year 1972-1973.
4.	The various government contributions to the Public Service Superannuation Account form part of government expenditure for each fiscal year and, accordingly, are detailed in the Appropriation and Expenditure section of Volume I of the Public Accounts. Furthermore, the government's responsibility to pay the benefits guaranteed by the legislation is recorded in the statement of Assets and Liabilities of the Public Accounts.
5.	Interest credited to the Public Service Superannuation Account is calculated on both employer and employee contributions.
6.	Total disbursements from the Public Service Superannuation Account were: (a) $107.7 million during the fiscal year 1970-1971; (b) $118.6 million during the fiscal year 1971-1972.
7.	Funds that are not needed for the immediate payment of pensions are invested, as required by law, in book liabilities of the government of Canada. They are used for the general purposes of the government of Canada in the same way as are the proceeds of the sale of government of Canada bonds. This is in accordance with parliament's acceptance of the procedures recommended by the Royal Commission on Government Organization.

What is the nature of and how many representations have been received by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or have been transmitted to him by colleagues in the Cabinet, since January 1, 1972 relative to a proposal for the national licensing of physicians and surgeons in Canada rather than preserving this jurisdiction to the provincial Colleges of Physicians and Surgeons?

speakeroldname: Hon. Marc Lalonde (Minister of National Health and Welfare):

subsubtopic: PROPOSAL FOR THE NATIONAL LICENSING OF PHYSICIANS AND SURGEONS IN CANADA

This was the basic reason for the establishment of the Medical Council of Canada.

Actually, we may have to feel our way a little to see whether the words in this amendment moved by the President of the Treasury Board actually carry into effect the words and the intent of the Minister of Finance.
Our concern about the proposal contained in the bill was that the motion would be put before the House and then be handled in accordance with the rules. The motion before the House could be considered for one day and, under the rules of the House, transferred to Government Orders. There it could lie in limbo ad infinitum. This was the trouble with the bill. This now overrides the effect of the
July 4, 1973

rules of the House. Once the motion has been tabled and, according to the rules, taken up, the debate must continue without interruption, outside of routine business, for three sitting days and then a decision taken. If the measure carries, the minister must bring in a bill without delay reflecting the intent of the motion. The bill will be immediately taken up the day after it is brought before the House. By the end of seven sitting days, all the stages of the bill shall have been considered, this also without interruption, if necessary.
The purport of the amendment is to make the review procedure more meaningful. Somewhere along the line there may be something that is still uncertain. Having considered the matter, we will have put what we want to the minister in order that the review procedure will be authoritative and meaningful. In so far as procedure is concerned, we have spelled it out. The review procedure, of course, must be based upon meaningful evidence. Therefore, the monitoring process that the minister described to the Leader of the Opposition and other members last night can stand even more suggestions. Some of my colleagues may have some to make this afternoon in that regard.
I want to be quite clear that under this tax provision, the review procedure is not a once and for all shot. If the government obtains other information from its monitoring or the opposition comes to the conclusion there must be a modification of this tax, any time after April 1, 1974 the necessary action may be taken. We will just have to see how this gets along. It may be that all of us will be surprised. The government may have grossly overestimated the effect of the inducement it has given to the manufacturing and processing sector of industry.
It is not a case that they will be able to quantify any payments out, because no payments are being made. The tax is being reduced, and the tax, of course, will be paid only some time in 1974. It is true there will be some periodic reporting by ceftain corporations but not by all of them. Many of the final tax returns of these companies will not come in until after April 1, 1974, and to this extent the information will not be available for the interim report. Certainly, though, we would hope that information will flow through more readily and that the Minister of Finance will organize his analysts so that they are in better shape than those of the Auditor General, who has an equally difficult monitoring task in many ways but who is unable to accomplish it for other reasons.
I hope the committee will agree to accept this amendment. We on this side are certainly prepared to do so. We feel that 60 is about the right number; it amounts to 25 per cent of the membership of this House, and a decision is within the control of the opposition. This is why we would accept the number 60, and we are not prepared to pay a numbers game in that connection.

Mr. Chairman, the purpose of my rising is to move an amendment which would effectively reduce the number of members required to call for a reassessment of this corporate tax bill next year from 60 to 25. I do this for a number of reasons.
First of all, on page 6 of the bill before us, sub-clause (3) stipulates that 60 members can sign a petition asking that the measure be either discontinued next year or that the reduction be reduced by any amount that parliament would like.
The purpose of the amendment is that in the current legislation it stipulates that 60 members must make that petition or request, and what we want to do in this party is reduce that number to 25 because we do not have confidence that the Conservative party will ask for such a review next year. We do not feel that party will have the intestinal fortitude to go ahead and ask that this measure be reviewed. If the number is reduced to 25 we are sure there will be a review of this corporate tax legislation next year.
The second reason we would like to move this amendment and have it carried by the House is that this party has no confidence in the review procedure the minister is establishing within his own department. We think the members of this House, representing the people of Canada, should make the decision about this corporate tax bill, since we could possibly make it immediately after the last day of March next year.
As I say, we in this party have no confidence in the review procedure because essentially that procedure is a sop to the Conservative party, a procedure by which bureaucrats in the Department of Finance are going to send out questionnaires and carry out surveys to determine whether the corporate tax cut is effective. I do not think this review procedure will have any validity at all.
The people who are handing out the tax cut will be interviewing and surveying those benefiting from it, and following those interviews and surveys the same people will make a decision as to whether this bill is effective. I should like to refer to Hansard of yesterday at page 5259 where a statement by the Minister of Finance appears. I want to quote a few sentences of the minister's answer to
July 4, 1973

questions by the opposition as to how the government will review and assess these corporate tax measures and the effect they will have on our economy. He said:
The following activities will be undertaken in making this assessment. First, we will be looking for the direct impact of the measures. The direct impact that the measures have had on existing companies or are likely to have will be examined by means of a questionnaire survey and interviews. Questionnaires will be sent to about 1,000 manufacturers and processing corporations representing several times as many establishments. It will include representation from all industrial segments, all regions of the country and virtually all sizes of corporations. This mailing will include all the largest firms in the country as well as a number of smaller companies.
Here we are sending out a questionnaire to the companies and corporations which are benefiting from the corporate tax cut from 49 per cent to 40 per cent. I would ask what kind of an assessment this will be. Will these companies receiving the benefits of this bill actually say to the Minister of Finance or the government that this bill is not good? Will they in all sincerity cut off the hand that feeds them? Perhaps this is like the skunk in the henhouse. This review procedure would be like asking the skunk. I am sure he would be in favour, but if you asked the chickens and the farmer you would get a totally different interpretation of the activity.
What we are trying to do through this amendment is in essence to survey the people of Canada. We want to ask the members of parliament to judge this activity next year, as soon as we can possibly make that judgment. I think the people of Canada, through their representatives, rather than a few bureaucrats in the Department of Finance, should be making this decision.
The minister then went on to state:
Interviews will be held with the 200 largest firms and about 25 medium and 25 small manufacturing and processing companies.
In addition to the questionnaire these people will interview some of the corporations about the effect of the corporation tax cuts and their impact on the economy. Then the minister states, and this is very interesting:
We anticipate that the companies' response to the new tax measures will be motivated in part by their expectation of increased cash flows-
Certainly these companies will be motivated in part by increased cash flows. They have had a tremendous year, a very profitable one so far, with an increase in the first three months of 53 per cent over the first three months last year, before taxes. Naturally these companies will be interested in maximizing their profits.
The Minister of Finance went on to say:
-but more importantly by a fundamental policy improvement designed to improve the investment climate in this country.
What guarantee do we have that the corporations will use this extra capital they will gain as a result of this tax cut to improve investment in new manufacturing and processing, creating more jobs in this country? I suggest there is absolutely no guarantee that these companies will use these funds for that purpose. They may elect to retain these extra earnings for some other purpose. They may decide to use them to modernize their plants by putting in new equipment which, indeed, in some cases may throw men out of work, creating fewer jobs rather than more. These corporations may decide to use these funds to pay
Income Tax Act (No. 2)
greater dividends to shareholders instead of investing in new manufacturing and processing in this country.
The minister has told the House that 60 per cent of the firms which will benefit from corporate tax cuts are foreign firms. Who is to say that some of the extra funds available to these companies will not actually end up in the hands of shareholders outside Canada? These companies may elect to send a greater portion of their profits to parent companies in the United States, or to pay out greater dividends to foreign shareholders. Again we have no guarantee in this legislation that these tax cuts will actually result in greater investment in this country and greater job creation here.
In addition, even if there were to be greater investment I do not think it would necessarily follow that if you have greater profits you will have greater investment: this has not been the fact in recent years. Last night I presented some statistics to the committee compiled by the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. They were compiled very recently and they relate to investment patterns in manufacturing and processing in this country. I do not mind repeating these statistics.
While manufacturing and processing corporations increased their profits in the last two years, investment in new manufacturing and processing in Canada actually declined. In 1970, for example, when corporation profits were considered to be lower than usual we found there was $3,223 million invested in new manufacturing and processing in Canada. In 1971 when corporation profits in Canada increased, if we follow the logic of the Liberal and Conservative policy investment should have increased, but it did not. Instead investment went down to $2,994 million. In 1972 profits again went up, but investment in new manufacturing and processing went down to $2,956 million.
To my mind and in the opinion of members of this party there is no guarantee that corporations will use the extra funds available for new investment in this country and for the creation of new jobs. I should like to hear some member of the Liberal or Conservative party prove that suggestion, or indicate some conclusive way to determine where these funds are actually going. The review procedure to be established by the government is a farce. The people who are drafting the policy will carry out a survey of those benefiting from it, and the conclusion of such a review procedure is a foregone conclusion.
I think this survey would be a whitewash job. That is why those of us in this party who are dedicated to the defeat of this bill want to try to keep control of the review of the bill as much as possible in the hands of this party or this Parliament, so that the people of Canada will be guaranteed that there will be a review of this bill.
I shall not repeat many of the things we have said in the past. We all know of the concern of our party. Profits have gone up. We know about the Shultz proposals in the United States. The minister states that they are just proposals, but we believe there is a strong possibility that some of them may come into effect. I suggest that the House should consider the amendment reducing the number of members from 60 to 25 in order to have an

Income Tax Act (No. 2)
automatic reassessment and review of the bill before us. The reason for this is not just because the review procedure is inadequate but because we believe the Conservative party may in the end chicken out. If that happens we want this access to possible control so that there will be a review of this bill because the members of this party demand the review.
If we do not do it ourselves, the members of the Conservative party may not insist upon the review and we would not have one at all. As a matter of fact, there is probably a conflict of interest in expecting the Conservative party to request a rescinding of this legislation, because it would be like cutting off the hand that feeds it. I am sure members of the Conservative party want to complain a little, but do not want to do anything about it.
I appeal to all members of this House, members of the Conservative party, the Liberal party and the Social Credit party, to support our amendment. Many members have expressed concern about the effect of this bill. Many of them have expressed concern about the review procedure. If they really mean what they say I hope they will support our amendment to reduce the number of members of parliament required to have this review from 60 to 25. Mr. Chairman, I should like to move the amendment. I move:

Mr. Chairman, let me deal with the first one first. I have recently received information from my colleague, the Minister of Justice in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board, concerning the possible delay in delivery of grain to the Canadian Wheat Board because of a peculiar interaction of the Canada Grain Act and the reporting of income on the cash basis under the Income Tax Act.
Under the Canada Grain Act farmers receive a cash purchase ticket which entitles the holder to cash at the time of receipt. As a result, the amount is included in income for tax purposes at that time. Even if the regulations under the Canada Grain Act were changed to provide for a deferral of the cash being received at the option of the farmer, the amount would still be treated as income at the time of delivery for income tax purposes.
I have been informed that this treatment will tend to encourage farmers to delay delivery of their grain near the end of their taxation year in years when there are good crops. This practice is to the detriment of the Canadian Wheat Board requirements and adversely affects the board's ability to meet its delivery commitments.
It is proposed to amend Section 76 of the Income Tax Act so that a farmer on the cash basis who delivers grain to the Canadian Wheat Board, and elects to defer receipt of the cash by taking a deferred payment purchase ticket, will only include the sale price in income when the cash is actually received.
In other words, that is an election open to the farmer. He can elect or not elect. I believe this amendment will reflect a more accurate "cash" method of reporting of income for grain producers and will place them in a more comparable position with other types of farming. This amendment
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
provides that where a taxpayer delivers grain to a primary elevator and receives a cash purchase ticket, but elects to receive payment for the delivery in the immediate subsequent taxation year, notwithstanding subsection 76(1) the amount of the sale will be included in income in the taxation year immediately following the taxation year in which the grain was delivered. The expressions "cash purchase ticket", "operator of an elevator" and "primary elevator" used in this section are defined in the Canada Grain Act and the expression "grain" has the meaning assigned by the Canadian Wheat Board Act.
I am wondering, Mr. Chairman, whether instead of reading the amendment I might just table it and ask that it be included in an appendix to Votes and Proceedings. If we make progress and get down to it I could introduce it in appropriate form at an appropriate stage. I am prepared to table copies in English and French of the proposed amendment to be circulated to members of the committee so that they will have time to digest it.

Mr. Chairman, it is complicated. Let us go back to subparagraphs (1)(i)(ii) and (vii). They each contain the same two amendments. The first amendment will prevent double accounting of certain amounts of a corporation's 1971 capital surplus on hand, and the second amendment merely allows one use of a section of the income tax application rules, 1971, also to have that effect for the purpose of computing the 1971 capital surplus on hand. Mr. Chairman, I would be glad to explain this clause. These amendments increase the basic exemption for single status from $1,500 to $1,600 and the additional exemption allowed to an individual who supports a spouse from $1,350 to $1,400. As a result of these amendments an individual of single status will not pay income tax until his income exceeds $1,600 which, with the $100 standard deduction, means $1,700.
An individual with full married status, for example a taxpayer who supports a spouse, who does not receive income in excess of $300 will not pay income tax until his income exceeds $1,600, plus $1,400, plus $100, or $3,100. I think that is the basis of the clause.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, while we are on this clause having to do with the exemption levels that are accorded to persons of single status and married status, can the minister of finance say whether any further consideration has been given to the situation that arises when both partners of a marriage are over 65? I hear the minister say "Ah". He has to give further thought to this. As he knows, this is a matter of concern about which members of parliament receive representations from taxpayers.
I realize the minister has come a reasonable piece by raising the extra exemption that is granted to those over 65 in two jumps, from $500 to $650 and now to $1,000, but it is still the case that that extra $1,000 is allowed only to the taxpayer. The kind of situation that turns up in many

letters I receive relates to the different treatment that is accorded to different married couples depending upon the source of their income.
I recognize that when married couples under the age of 65 are both working a case can be made for a higher total exemption to be enjoyed by them. However, when the husband and wife are both over 65, should it matter whether the income is all in the name of one of the partners or both? If the income is in the name of one partner only, the amount of exemption allowed will be $3,100 plus $1,000, or $4,100. However, if the married couple is in the situation where the retirement income comes partly to one and partly to the other, whether 50/50 or on some other basis, each of them can enjoy a total of $2,700, namely $1,600, plus $100, plus $1,000, for a total of $5,400. My question is, should that difference obtain?
In the case where the wife does not have the income, modern theory says she helped her husband earn his pension status and pension rights. However, if all the money comes in his name, the exemption level is only $4,100. If they manage it so that the money comes in both names, the exemption level can be $5,400. As a matter of fact, in the case of a couple where all the income is in one name, even that $4,100 can be reduced by the amount of the spouse's old age security over a certain figure. There can be cases where the exemption is $4,100 or less and cases where the exemption is $5,400.
I think of the instance where neither is working. They are both retired. They both receive old age security and other forms of pension income. Surely they worked together to produce this situation, whether one was in the home or both were out working. Is there not a case for some sort of equality being established with respect to the income tax exemption level in cases where both spouses are over 65?

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I suppose the brief answer is that the hon. member is dealing with what is in effect a family unit style of taxing income. We are some distance from that. I might say to him that since I have been Minister of Finance we have raised the level of income for a married couple, where the taxpayer is 65 or over, on which no tax is paid by $500 in the past year and a half, form $3,600 to $4,100. I am conscious of the fact that when we are dealing with exemptions from income, we are dealing with that part of the older population that has deprived itself during lifetime of the ability to consume in order to save for their retirement. I am very conscious about making sure we are fair in this regard. The family unit concept or joint income is a concept that will need a lot further study before I can give any immediate contemplation to the hon. member's suggestion, but I know what he has in mind.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I do not wish to detract by one iota from the Oscar the minister has awarded himself by telling us that in the past year and a half the extra income allowed to a married couple has been increased by $500. In fact, I will give him another Oscar. For some married couples, the exemption has been increased by $1,000, $500 to each. That is the whole point of my intervention. I think the minister understands that this relates to the concept of a family
July 4, 1973

income. He admits it has to be studied. He looks at his high priced help in front of him and says, "you better study this". This is the sort of answer we get to these questions year in and year out. Even assistant deputy ministers will some day be retired on pensions. They have wives.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: They are immortal!

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
They retire and receive pensions for themselves and their wives. Maybe by that time they will hire themselves out as consultants as to what should be done, and as to what they did not improve when they were in the department.
In days when we are very conscious of the principle of equality between men and women, there should not be this tax discrimination against wives who stayed home. The wife who stayed home made a contribution to the income and the pension status of her husband. She should not be discriminated against in terms of tax law as compared with the wife who went out to work or inherited some money and has a pension income for herself.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, if that argument has any validity-and I do not want to get into the profundity of it for the moment-it has validity throughout married life, not only at the pension age. We are dealing with a fundamental concept that will have to be looked at in general terms.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have no objection to the minister carrying the profundity of this all the way.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to look at the other side of this. I know the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has a great desire to put everybody in the same bag and paint them all the same shade of green. He is a great one for the principle of total legality for all, regardless of effort. I have received many complaints from people who ask what is the use of being careful, saving and investing. All that happens is that under the Income Tax Act they are being increasingly penalized and placed in a less favourable position compared with those who did not save. It has to be admitted that some of that latter did not have an opportunity to save, but, let's face it, many people today spend money as they make it regardless of the future. Those others who are careful, or good managers, are penalized.
Let me say this: there is many a wife today who during her senior years possesses a tidy nest egg because she happens to be an astute businesswoman, even though she might not have been obliged to go out to earn. If we propose to consider people who have been careful, I am prepared to say that this differential can be considered a bonus for thrift and I thoroughly agree there should be some sort of incentive.
I remember during the last election campaign several older women, still married, crying into the telephone, actually crying, because their small incomes, money they had scrimped and saved for, and denied themselves for, and which they had invested, was being eaten away in one
Income Tax Law (No. 3)
way or another, whereas those who had nothing and were dependent on the state were getting cost of living bonuses, non-taxable guaranteed income supplements and increases in pensions. Yet the person who had striven hard to save was being increasingly taxed.
I thoroughly agree with this point of view because today there is a philosophy around in government which amounts to this: save now, we will tax you later. I think it is one of the least attractive features of our taxation policy that people who have been careful and who have invested their money should be treated in this way. It may be they have invested in government bonds. A good deal of this money is in government bonds, and there is nothing more patriotic than that, as the Minister of Finance would be the first to agree. On the other hand, the investment could have been in Canadian equities, all sorts of things. We have devised ways and means of separating elderly people from their hard-earned savings. So I consider that at the present time a differential is quite appropriate.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
I rise to support the argument put forward by my hon. friend from Winnipeg North Centre. The same circumstances have been brought to my attention many times by farm wives, particularly in Saskatchewan. These women work very hard though they may not actually share in the ownership of the farm, which would be registered in the name of the husband. But they work very hard alongside their husbands. If a farm wife does not own part of the farm, that is, if part of the farm is not in her name, the exemption would amount to $3,100. Otherwise, it is $3,400. So there is a difference of $300.
I hope the minister will look at this situation and bring in an amendment next year, or as soon as possible. The same applies to the situation of a wife in a working class home. Many of these wives stay home to look after domestic affairs and family; as a result, they are discriminated against when it comes to claiming exemptions on their tax forms. I believe the minister should consider making amendments of the kind I have in mind as soon as possible in the hope of creating a more egalitarian society.

subtopic: STATUTE LAW RELATING TO INCOME TAX (No. 3)
speechtext:
I should like to say a word about the subject raised by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni. I give the minister full credit for the changes he has made in the exemptions I presume they will be worth something in the next election. But having been here through seven or eight elections I can only say I should like to see a number of changes introduced to benefit the workers, and I should like to see them made a lot faster than has been the case in the last ten years.
I, too, receive a good many letters about taxation problems, not so much from elderly ladies-they usually go to somebody else-as from workers who have to travel 50 or 60 miles each day to earn their living and who object strongly to the fact that no allowance is available to them in this regard. They think it is unreasonable that concessions made to one segment of workers do not apply to another. This applies to the construction field, particularly when men live away from home and are obliged to incur additional expenses from Monday to Friday. Others live away for three or four months at a time yet have to maintain homes, in the same way as members of parliament are so often called upon to do.

July 4, 1973

Then there is the question of the equipment allowance which has recently been available. When it was sought, years ago, we were thinking in terms of oilers and rubbers for miners, about specialized clothing for workers in various industries. Over the years a need has developed for more elaborate equipment; for example, chain saws which are not only desirable but absolutely necessary for some tasks. Originally workers used company equipment to do these jobs. Today these services have expanded, and a worker may provide expensive equipment, particularly in the forest industry; for example, a tree loading machine, or one of those elaborate machines that trim leaves, saw the timber, cut it into lengths and pile it. Such equipment costs tens of thousands of dollars and is supplied by a person who is not really a jobber in the sense of being in the business of supplying equipment. Previously, the companies supplied this or similar equipment.
It seems to me that if a person earns his income by working with equipment of this kind he should be entitled to an allowance just as if he were incorporated and hiring other people to operate the machines. I am speaking of a new development which has taken place only recently.
It seems to me that the Minister of Finance, without really being very generous to the workers of the country, could give consideration to these three problems: transportation allowances, living away from home allowances, and equipment allowances. This would allow a much more equitable relationship among the workers in various areas.
For some time living allowances away from home have been granted to transport workers working on the railways. As a result they have been able to claim transportation costs while working away from home. During the same time many people have had to drive 40 or 50 miles to get to their jobs, and they have not been allowed to claim these expenses.
It seems to me that the minister should look at this situation and perhaps move an amendment to the ways and means motion. There is a great disparity between exemptions allowed people in one industry and those allowed to people in others. I receive many letters of complaint because of these disparities. One man might say his neighbour has a similar job in a different industry and is allowed an exemption for transportation costs which he is not allowed. Another individual might say he only needs a saw and a hammer to perform his job and is allowed an exemption. His neighbour will complain that he has an expenditure of thousands of dollars for the equipment he requires to perform his work, but he is not allowed this exemption. It seems to me that if an individual incorporates he receives the exemption.
We also give allowances to operators of small stores who put signs in their windows offering free home delivery. These men can write off transportation costs but another storekeeper who does not put up a similar sign must pay his own delivery costs.
These inequities should be considered. We should even out things for everybody by either cutting them out altogether or making them available to all. I am sure the minister would agree that he receives thousands of requests for information about these provisions for

exemptions which are not provided on an equitable basis. This seems to be an area in which the minister has made some small endeavour. I would like to see that endeavour made for everyone, covering expenses of all workers.
This is most important in view of changing circumstances in the last few years. Many people drive 40 or 50 miles to get to parliament here in Ottawa. Often members of parliament have to drive 30 or 40 miles to this city because they cannot afford accommodation here. I think a similar problem is faced by workers in industry. I am not making a pitch for members of parliament, but this is the fact. I think those workers who have to do this should be given some consideration. If these allowances are made for workers in certain sections of industry, they should be made for all.
